overview.text: Differentiation is the calculus process of finding a derivative, which describes how a function’s output changes as its input changes. At a particular input, the derivative is the instantaneous rate of change and, on a graph, the slope of the tangent line there. It is defined as the limit of slopes between nearby points—the difference quotient—when that limit exists; writing f′(x) describes the derivative as a new function of x. Derivatives turn changing quantities into useful rates: for example, differentiating a position function gives instantaneous velocity. A function must be continuous to be differentiable at a point, but continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability.

key_facts.text: The derivative at x = a is defined by the limit f′(a) = limₕ→₀ [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h, if the limit exists; the fraction is called the difference quotient.
Geometrically, f′(a) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph at (a, f(a)).
The derivative function is commonly written f′(x); other notations include dy/dx and df/dx.
A derivative’s units are output units divided by input units; for a position function measured over time, the derivative represents instantaneous velocity.
Differentiability implies continuity, but not the reverse: |x| is continuous at zero yet has no derivative there.
